newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq says it barred U.N. team from security sites.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says it barred U.N. team from security sites.

text.p: Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz has accused some U.N. arms inspectors of trying to probe into Iraq's security apparatus, the official Iraqi News Agency reported on Tuesday.
It said he complained in a letter to the U.N. Security Council chief about inspections by the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) in charge of overseeing the destruction of Iraq's prohibited weapons.
He said Iraq had banned U.N. inspectors from entering three sites last week because they were sensitive for security reasons.

"We have serious concern that the entry into these sites does not aim to implement the mandate of the Special Commission...but to make use of the facilities available to the Special Commission as a cover to detect the security systems of Iraq ...and the security of its leadership," Aziz said, according to INA.
UNSCOM chairman Rolf Ekeus complained last week to the U.N. Security Council that Iraq blocked a U.N. team from two suspected military sites on Thursday and a third location on Wednesday.
Aziz named the locations as Iraqi intelligence service headquarters and presidential sites.
"Colonel Scott Ritter...requested to enter the office of the political section in the Intelligence Service which contains the secrets of this service. We did not allow him to do so.

"Colonel Ritter requested to go to a site related to the security of the Presidency which had been already inspected twice...This time we did not allow him to do so," Aziz said. Ritter is an American.
Aziz accused the United States of trying to use UNSCOM to implement its hostile policy.

"Colonel Ritter, the chief inspector who insisted without any justification on the entry into these sites, is an officer in the U.S. Army," Aziz said, adding that the Council was "aware of the United States' position towards Iraq and its political regime".
Aziz said Iraq allowed the team to inspect 40 sites, which he listed in the letter, and banning the team from three sites should not lead to describing Iraq as "uncooperative".

The Council deplored on Friday what it called unacceptable interference by Iraq with the flight of U.N. helicopters working with the weapons inspection team and told Baghdad to take immediate steps to halt such actions.
The Council is expected to deal with the three incidents after being briefed by Ekeus this week, and sources at the Council said a formal resolution was likely to be adopted.
